The questionnaire helps distinguish practical task relevance from evidence of broader engineering competence. reinterpretations[0]:

The questionnaire usefully separates documentation, scoring validity and broader interpretation. Multi-part questions can obscure different findings: marking checks occurred, but their coverage and consistency remain uncertain. Item 15 warrants Yes because setup changes were tested. Item 11 concerns support for weighting, so documenting equal weights alone is insufficient. Fairness judgments should specify whether the comparison concerns an AI alone or an AI together with its retrieval system.

instrument_review:
DesignQA is reviewed using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 2025. The reviewed scope is the original benchmark described in the 2024 paper and its public scoring software. Practical vehicle materials support task relevance, while documented scoring sensitivities and unequal information supply complicate comparisons. Reliability and broader engineering interpretations remain insufficiently established. Section-level judgments are not combined into an aggregate quality score.

instrument_review:
DesignQA is reviewed using the supplied EFPA 2025 model, with AI systems and their information-supply pipelines as assessed units. The evidence supports examining performance on the specified Formula SAE tasks; broader engineering competence and fine ranking differences remain unresolved. Ratings use the original key: n/a = inapplicable, 0 = insufficient evidence to rate, 1 = inadequate, 2 = adequate, 3 = good, 4 = excellent. Section judgments are qualitative, not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 presents example grid transformations and asks AI systems to produce exact outputs for unfamiliar inputs. This review covers its public test problems, inspected official scoring software and ARC Prize verified-testing rules. Evidence supports describing performance on these grid tasks under recorded conditions; broader reasoning interpretations remain unresolved. All numbered EFPA descriptive fields and evaluation items are addressed below, including section-specific overall ratings. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

supported_claims[0]:

Part A general description: ARC-AGI-2 measures success on unfamiliar two-dimensional grid transformations using worked examples and exact output matching. The benchmark supplies development puzzles and three evaluation sets with different access restrictions. Human puzzle-solving informed difficulty matching. Verified evaluations constrain settings and spending, while public scoring awards partial problem credit when only some new inputs are solved. No distinct skill scales or norm-based score transformations are described.

documented_problems[3]:

documented_problems[4]:
10.3.2; final evaluation: The supplied studies concern grid problems. They do not establish prediction of language performance, social interaction or real-world work.

instrument_review:
DesignQA evaluates answers about Formula SAE rules, vehicle images and drawings using 1,451 question-answer pairs in six uneven groups. This review covers the original 2024 paper and public scoring software described in the supplied passage. Scores describe performance of AI systems together with their information supply and marking conditions; broader engineering competence remains unresolved. All numbered EFPA descriptive fields and evaluation items are addressed below. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

supported_claims[22]:
Part A general description: DesignQA asks AI systems to retrieve rules, explain terms, identify components and evaluate dimensional or functional compliance using one Formula SAE rulebook and vehicle materials. Six task groups use different marking methods. The public software combines groups with equal weights despite their unequal sizes. Public materials permit partial inspection, while exact historical replication of every reported result is not established.

documented_problems[0]:
6.1.3.1=1; 6.1.3.3=1: One rulebook, limited task types and a distribution dominated by 1,192 individual-rule questions provide inadequate design support for a broad engineering-understanding interpretation. This judgement does not deny usefulness for the sampled tasks.

documented_problems[1]:
3.2; 7.1.7=1: The passage documents missing-comma penalties, valid related rules absent from supplied answers and a released answer file with fewer rows than the corresponding paper count. These are substantive scoring/content concerns; their overall frequency is unknown.

documented_problems[2]:
3.2; 6.3.4: Equal weighting combines different marking methods and highly unequal group sizes without evidence that the resulting number measures a distinct skill.

documented_problems[3]:
9.7: Five runs with different passage sets do not isolate variation under identical conditions. The 16-question performance group changes by 6.25 percentage points for one additional correct answer.

documented_problems[4]:
10.2.3; 11.5: Different systems receive different information. Their comparisons concern the AI plus its retrieval/input arrangement, rather than an isolated model capability.

documented_problems[5]:
10.4.1; 10.4.2=1; 10.4.3=1: The described scale-bar drawings all comply with the rule, so always answering yes would earn their yes/no credit. This supports concern about unintended scoring routes, without showing any tested AI used that strategy or invalidating separately scored explanations.

documented_problems[6]:
5.1; 6.2.4: Exact historical software, settings and inputs are not fully linked to each result. Identifiable code revisions lack a clear account of their score effects.

documented_problems[7]:
10.5; final evaluation: Real vehicle materials establish task relevance but do not demonstrate prediction of performance on other standards or real engineering projects.

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 is reviewed using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 2025, version 5.0, attributed to EFPA, https://www.efpa.eu/, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the supplied benchmark passages and model extraction were used; the authoritative PDF was not inspected. Ratings retain EFPA meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient evidence; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are qualitative, not averaged; no aggregate quality score is calculated. Final evaluation: public grid tasks and specified scoring support examination of performance under recorded conditions. Development procedures and scoring examples are strengths; public exposure, material corrections and unresolved AI score precision limit interpretation. Reliability and validity are critical attributes rated 0, so EFPA guidance restricts use to research or exceptional circumstances involving highly skilled experts; this is an evidence limitation, not demonstrated poor performance. Conclusions: use for research comparisons of grid-task performance, with expertise in evaluation conditions, scoring and exposure risks. Broad intelligence claims and small differences between systems remain unsupported by this packet; supplier qualification requirements and future research plans are not supplied.

instrument_review:
DesignQA is reviewed using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 2025, version 5.0, attributed to EFPA, https://www.efpa.eu/, CC BY-SA 4.0. Only the supplied benchmark passages and model extraction were used; the authoritative PDF was not inspected. Ratings retain EFPA meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient evidence; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are qualitative, not averaged; no aggregate quality score is calculated. Final evaluation: authentic Formula SAE materials and six task groups support examination of bounded engineering-document performance. Documented scoring sensitivity, an exploitable compliant-only subset and unequal information supply constrain comparisons. Reliability and validity are critical attributes rated 0; EFPA guidance therefore restricts use to research or exceptional circumstances involving highly skilled experts, without treating missing evidence as demonstrated poor quality. Conclusions: use for research on the stated tasks with explicit system, retrieval, input and software conditions. Broad engineering competence and close rankings require more evidence. Users need expertise in engineering content and AI evaluation; supplier qualification requirements and future development plans are unspecified.

instrument_review: ARC-AGI-2 provides grid puzzles for comparing AI systems’ performance at inferring rules from examples. Public tasks, inspected scoring tests and verified-testing rules support a bounded evaluation of this performance. Repeatability, equivalence of test sets for AI systems and broader interpretations of reasoning remain unresolved in the supplied passages. This review applies the original EFPA model from the requested AI-familiar, benchmark-new perspective; it is not an expert certification or EFPA endorsement.
closing_note: Unclear questions concern how human norms, disability access, qualified administration and interpretive reports map to AI evaluation. These mappings are recorded explicitly. The scoring distinction between partial problem credit and 'fully solved' also requires careful wording.

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 provides grid puzzles for comparing AI systems’ performance at inferring rules from examples. Public tasks, inspected scoring tests and verified-testing rules support a bounded evaluation of this performance. Repeatability, equivalence of test sets for AI systems and broader interpretations of reasoning remain unresolved in the supplied passages. This review applies the original EFPA model from the requested AI-familiar, benchmark-new perspective; it is not an expert certification or EFPA endorsement.

instrument_review: DesignQA compares AI systems on engineering-document questions using Formula SAE rules and vehicle materials. Its practical content and public materials support inspection of performance on the stated tasks. Documented scoring sensitivity, uneven groups, different information supplies and incomplete historical records limit interpretation. Evidence for repeatability and broader engineering competence remains insufficient. This review uses the original EFPA model from the requested AI-familiar, benchmark-new perspective and does not imply expert certification or EFPA endorsement.

These interpretations are explicit. Competence thresholds must also be distinguished from engineering rules used within individual questions.

instrument_review:
DesignQA compares AI systems on engineering-document questions using Formula SAE rules and vehicle materials. Its practical content and public materials support inspection of performance on the stated tasks. Documented scoring sensitivity, uneven groups, different information supplies and incomplete historical records limit interpretation. Evidence for repeatability and broader engineering competence remains insufficient. This review uses the original EFPA model from the requested AI-familiar, benchmark-new perspective and does not imply expert certification or EFPA endorsement.

documented_problems[3]:

documented_problems[4]:

documented_problems[5]:
7.1.7; 10.4.3: All described scale-bar drawings comply with the rule. Always answering 'yes' would earn decision credit on that portion; the passages do not show that any tested AI used this strategy.

documented_problems[6]:
2.11; 9.7.3: In the 16-question performance group, one additional correct answer changes accuracy by 6.25 percentage points. Fine comparisons need precision evidence.

documented_problems[7]:
5.1; 6.2.2: One released answer file has fewer rows than the corresponding paper question count. Exact historical software, inputs and settings are not fully linked to every result.

documented_problems[8]:
Final evaluation: One rulebook and limited task coverage constrain generalisation. The authors acknowledge that performance on another technical document remains uncertain.

reinterpretations[0]:

reinterpretations[3]:
9—Repeatability means rerunning the same AI configuration under the same conditions. Human study participant counts and session counts are not converted into AI reliability sample sizes. Internal consistency is not imposed on heterogeneous tasks; alternative precision evidence remains necessary.

reinterpretations[4]:

reinterpretations[5]:

reinterpretations[6]:
Final evaluation—Reliability and broader-interpretation validity are marked critical. Under EFPA, their 0 ratings restrict supported recommendations to research or exceptional expert use; they denote insufficient evidence, not demonstrated poor performance.

reinterpretations[7]:
Instrument fidelity—All original sections A, B and C are retained. EFPA's section judgments are reported without calculating an aggregate score or implying EFPA endorsement.

instrument_review:
DesignQA review using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 2025, version 5.0, from the perspective of an AI user new to benchmarks. Scope: the original benchmark described in the 2024 paper and its public scoring software. Ratings follow EFPA: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient evidence to rate; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are qualitative, not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated. Every numbered descriptive field and rated item is addressed below; no substantive items are intentionally omitted. Findings apply only to the supplied passages.

supported_claims[0]:
Part A, 1—Instrument name and short name: DesignQA. Original paper year: 2024. Developers are described as researchers and engineers working with Formula SAE materials. Source inspection date: 6 October 2026.

supported_claims[1]:
2.1—Content keywords: engineering-rule retrieval, drawing understanding, rule application. 2.2—Area: AI evaluation using engineering tasks. 2.3—Intended population: AI systems answering questions about engineering documents and vehicle materials. 2.4—Main users: people comparing AI systems; formal user categories are not specified.

supported_claims[2]:
2.5—Six question-group scores and a software-generated overall score. The groups concern individual-rule retrieval, related-rule retrieval, technical terms, component presence, dimensions and functional performance. Their status as distinct underlying skills is unestablished.

supported_claims[3]:
2.6—Digital text responses. 2.8—Conditions include model-specific instructions, settings and information supply; systems may receive a whole rulebook or retrieved passages. 2.9—Open text and yes/no responses, sometimes with explanations. 2.10—Stimuli include written rules, vehicle images and drawings.

supported_claims[4]:
2.11—The paper reports 1,451 question-answer pairs. Individual-rule retrieval has 1,192 questions; functional performance has 16. 2.12.1—Individual administration, reinterpreted as evaluating one AI configuration. 2.16—A fixed released question collection is described; changing retrieved passages is an administration variation rather than demonstrated adaptive testing. 2.17—Other informant: the AI provides task responses.

supported_claims[5]:
3.1—Digital scoring. 3.2—Scoring combines answer-text similarity and yes/no correctness; explanations may receive separate similarity scores. The software weights the six groups equally for an overall score. 3.3—Other scales: group-level task scores and a combined score using different marking methods. 3.4—n/a: no standard-score transformation is described. 3.5—No differentiated norms are supplied.

supported_claims[6]:
5.1—Supporting materials include the paper, public questions, instructions, scoring code, some AI responses, small marking-test files and code history. 5.2—Public digital materials are described.

supported_claims[7]:
General description—DesignQA asks AI systems to retrieve and apply rules, explain terms and interpret vehicle images or drawings from Formula SAE materials. The original paper reports 1,451 question-answer pairs in six uneven groups. Answers may be open text or yes/no with explanations. Marking uses text similarity and decision correctness; public software also combines the groups with equal weight. Evaluated systems sometimes receive different information supplies. The benchmark provides evidence about these particular engineering-document tasks, while transfer to other technical documents and real engineering projects remains uncertain.

supported_claims[8]:

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 is reviewed using the supplied EFPA 2025 model, retaining its descriptive fields and rating scale. The evidence supports describing performance on unfamiliar grid problems under specified evaluation conditions. It does not establish repeatability of AI scores or their meaning for broader intelligence. This is a simulated review from the requested perspective, not an expert accreditation. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

instrument_review:
Condition-native review of ARC-AGI-2 using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 5.0 (2025), Parts A–C. Perspective: familiar with AI use, new to benchmarks; this is a recorded AI review simulation. Evidence is limited to the supplied ARC passages. Ratings retain EFPA meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated. All numbered fields and rated items are addressed below, including conditional subareas. This is not EFPA endorsement.

supported_claims[0]:
Part A, 1: Instrument name and short name: ARC-AGI-2. Scope: public test problems, official scoring software, and rules for evaluations ARC Prize runs or verifies. Developers: ARC Prize Foundation staff and partners; the supplied figure credits François Chollet and colleagues. Sources were inspected on 7 October 2026; this is not a publication or review date.

supported_claims[1]:
2.1: Other—rule inference, grid problem solving, reasoning. 2.2: Other—AI evaluation and research. 2.3: Intended assessed population: AI systems solving unfamiliar grid problems. 2.4: Intended users are not explicitly specified; the passages discuss researchers and verified evaluators.

supported_claims[2]:
2.5: One reported problem-solving score; no separately established skill scales. 2.6: Other—software-mediated grid outputs. 2.8: Verified evaluations specify AI settings and a spending limit, record settings, and use one run; other testing routes may differ.

supported_claims[3]:
2.9: Production-based responses—output grids. 2.10: Coloured grids; the supplied illustration is described in words. 2.11: 1,000 development problems and three test sets of 120 problems each; problems may contain multiple new inputs.

supported_claims[4]:
2.12.1: Reinterpreted individual administration—one AI system configuration evaluated per run. 2.12.2: Verified administration is controlled through ARC Prize policies; public access alone does not establish controlled execution. 2.13: Software execution is required; exact device and connectivity requirements are not supplied.

supported_claims[5]:
2.15: Public, semi-private and private sets differ in access and were selected for similar human difficulty; development problems serve practice. ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 are separate versions. 2.16: Static released problems; no response-adaptive selection is described. 2.17: Other—the assessed AI produces responses; these are performance outputs rather than self-reports.

supported_claims[6]:
3.1: Digital scoring of AI outputs. 3.2: Two attempts per new input; an exact size-and-colour match earns input credit. Input credits are averaged within each problem, then problem scores are averaged. 3.3: Other—mean problem score based on exact-match input credits. 3.4: n/a; no standard-score transformation is described. 3.5: No differentiated norms are supplied in these passages.

supported_claims[7]:
4.1: Digitally produced scores and released testing outputs are described; a distinct interpretive report product and number of report types are not established. 4.2: Closest report analogue: testing outputs, costs, times and problem scores. 4.4: Other—task and problem-score summaries. 4.8: The described scoring rule links answers transparently to scores, although the complete output archive was not checked. 4.9: Other—observed puzzle-solving results and execution information.

supported_claims[8]:
5.1: Supporting materials include public problems, a technical report, rules, software, marking tests and a dated change record. 5.2: Public digital materials are described; exact publication formats are not fully specified.

supported_claims[9]:
General description: ARC-AGI-2 presents worked pairs of coloured grids and asks an AI to infer a rule and complete new grids. Development and evaluation problems are separated. Its three evaluation sets were matched using human difficulty information. Official scoring averages exact-match credits within problems and then across problems. Verified results concern a specified configuration and spending limit. Broader reasoning claims extend beyond the supplied grid-task evidence.

instrument_review:
Condition-native review of the original DesignQA benchmark using the supplied EFPA Test Review Model 5.0 (2025), Parts A–C. Perspective: familiar with AI use, new to benchmarks; this is a recorded AI review simulation. Evidence is limited to the supplied DesignQA passages. Ratings retain EFPA meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated. All numbered fields and rated items are addressed below, including conditional subareas. This is not EFPA endorsement.

supported_claims[0]:
Part A, 1: Instrument name and short name: DesignQA. Scope: the original benchmark described in the 2024 paper and its public scoring software. Creators are described as researchers and engineers; individual names and publisher identities are not supplied. Sources were inspected on 6 October 2026, which is not the review date. Original paper year: 2024; exact benchmark publication date is not supplied.

supported_claims[1]:
2.1: Other—engineering rule retrieval, technical-document understanding, design assessment. 2.2: Other—AI evaluation using Formula SAE engineering materials. 2.3: Intended assessed population: AI systems answering questions about rules and vehicle materials. 2.4: Main intended user categories are not explicitly stated.

supported_claims[2]:
2.5: Six task groups: individual-rule retrieval, related-rule retrieval, terminology explanation, component presence, dimensions and functional performance. Separate group scores and an equally weighted overall score are produced; distinct underlying skills are not established.

supported_claims[3]:
2.6: Other—software-mediated text and yes/no answers, sometimes explanations. 2.8: Systems receive specified instructions and settings, but some receive a full rulebook and others retrieved passages. Their information-supply arrangements are part of the evaluated system.

supported_claims[4]:
2.9: Open production responses and yes/no selection responses. 2.10: Text, vehicle images and drawings. 2.11: 1,451 question-and-answer pairs in six uneven groups; 1,192 individual-rule questions and 16 functional-performance questions. Counts for the other four groups are not supplied.

supported_claims[5]:
2.12.1: Reinterpreted individual administration—an AI configuration is evaluated. 2.12.2: Researcher-specified conditions are described, but exact correspondence to EFPA supervision categories is unclear. 2.13: Digital execution and access to relevant materials are required; exact devices and connectivity are unspecified.

supported_claims[6]:
2.15: Six task groups may be reported separately; no equivalent alternate forms are established. Later question/software changes are mentioned, without a full version inventory. 2.16: Released question content is treated as static; changing retrieved context is not established as adaptive item selection. 2.17: Other—the AI supplies performance responses rather than self-reports.

supported_claims[7]:
3.1: Digital scoring of AI responses. 3.2: Multiple methods include wording similarity and yes/no accuracy, with some explanation scores. The overall score weights all six groups equally. 3.3: Other—accuracy, text-similarity measures and an equally weighted composite. 3.4: n/a; no standard-score transformation described. 3.5: No differentiated norms supplied.

supported_claims[8]:
4.1: Software-produced overall and group scores are available; a separate interpretive report product and number of report types are not established. 4.2: Closest report analogue: group and overall result summaries. 4.4: Other—task-group and composite scores. 4.8: Aggregate weighting is explained, while a complete answer-to-credit and score-to-interpretation link is not established. 4.9: Other—observed task performance.

supported_claims[9]:
5.1: Supporting materials include a paper, public questions, instructions, scoring code, small marking-test files, some AI responses and code history. 5.2: Public digital materials are described; exact publication formats are incompletely specified.

supported_claims[10]:
General description: DesignQA evaluates AI answers to questions grounded in a Formula SAE rulebook, vehicle images, drawings and test data. Six groups cover retrieval, terminology and design checks. Responses are marked using several methods, and group scores receive equal weight in the composite. Reported comparisons concern both the AI and its supplied information. Results on other technical documents remain uncertain.

supported_claims[11]:
6.1.1 = 2; 6.2.1 = 3: Tasks have an understandable connection to engineering-document work, while broader engineering understanding is not fully operationalised.

supported_claims[12]:
6.1.3, 6.1.3.1 = 2; 6.1.3.2 = 2: Real engineering sources, practitioner contributions and question review support the task design, with incomplete coverage and review details. 6.1.5: Framework not specified; group counts, illustrative scoring issues and score comparisons are described, but standard item indices are not supplied.

supported_claims[13]:
6.2.2 = 2; 6.2.7 = 2: Sources and question-checking procedures are explained, including review exceptions, but expert qualifications and agreement are not fully reported. 6.2.13 = 3: The supplied explanation is understandable without engineering expertise; this rating does not cover all original materials.

supported_claims[14]:
6.3.1 = 2; 6.3.4 = 2: The packet describes inputs, instructions, system conditions and appropriate limits on interpretation. 6.3.10 = 2; 6.4 = 2: Available instructions explain the basic evaluation and major limitations, but leave reproduction and technical guidance incomplete.

supported_claims[15]:
7.1.2 = 2; 7.1.3 = 2; 7.1.4 = 2: Question types, response requirements and supporting materials are explained sufficiently for a limited task-usability judgment.

supported_claims[16]:
10.1: As EFPA directs, content evidence is considered with development under section 6. Authentic engineering materials support relevance to the sampled tasks, without demonstrating coverage across engineering industries.

supported_claims[17]:
10.3.1.1: Differences between AI systems and other context/input comparisons are described. 10.3.1.6 = 2: Changes to passages, labels, scale bars and highlighting provide limited experimental evidence about task influences; they do not establish broad engineering competence.

supported_claims[18]:
10.4.1: Other—analyses and discussion of formatting, retrieval quality, component familiarity and exposure. 10.4.2 = 2; 10.4.3 = 2: These identify relevant influences and limitations, but do not comprehensively exclude unintended routes to credit.

supported_claims[19]:
Part C: Sources used are the supplied DesignQA passages and supplied EFPA model. EFPA attribution: European Federation of Psychologists’ Associations AISBL, 2025, Model for the Review, Description and Evaluation of Psychological and Educational Tests, version 5.0; https://www.efpa.eu/; CC BY-SA 4.0. No external bibliography was consulted.

documented_problems[0]:
6.1.3.3 = 1; 6.1.8 = 1: Selection leaves strongly uneven task coverage, a limited engineering domain and a described scale-bar portion containing only compliant designs. These weaken support for the stated broad assessment purpose despite authentic source materials.

documented_problems[1]:
6.3.2 = 1: Documented examples show that missing commas and valid related rules absent from the reference answer can affect credit. Scoring therefore sometimes responds to answer presentation or reference incompleteness.

documented_problems[2]:
7.1.7 = 1; 7.1.8 = 1: The all-compliant scale-bar portion permits a constant 'yes' response to earn its decision credit, and a released answer file has fewer rows than the paper's corresponding question count. These are concrete material concerns, not a measured overall error rate.

documented_problems[3]:
3.2; 10.2: Equal weighting gives the 16-question performance group the same composite weight as the 1,192-question individual-rule group. The passages do not justify this as measurement of a common skill.

documented_problems[4]:
2.8; 6.2.4 = 1: Systems receive different information supplies, and historical settings, inputs and software are not fully linked to each result. Comparisons represent system-plus-information performance, with incomplete reproduction records.

documented_problems[5]:
9.7; 10.5: One extra correct answer changes accuracy by 6.25 percentage points in the 16-question group. This makes fine comparisons sensitive to individual responses; it is not itself a reliability coefficient.

documented_problems[6]:
10.4.3: Always answering 'yes' would obtain the decision credit on the described compliant scale-bar portion. There is no evidence that any tested AI used this strategy.

documented_problems[7]:
Final evaluation: Strengths are authentic materials, explicit task categories, public inspection opportunities and acknowledged limitations. Concrete scoring and content defects constrain broader interpretation. Critical qualities are scoring correctness, score precision and validity for engineering-understanding claims. EFPA's critical 0/1 guidance supports research use or exceptional expert-led use for those claims, with task-level inspection and explicit conditions.

instrument_review:
Condition-native review of the original DesignQA benchmark described in the 2024 paper and its public scoring software, using only the supplied passage. EFPA 2025 Parts A–C are retained; adaptations are explicit. Ratings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient evidence to rate; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section judgments are not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

supported_claims[0]:
Part A, 1: Instrument name: DesignQA. Original benchmark paper: 2024. Developers: researchers and engineers; individual names and institutions are not supplied. Sources inspected: 6 October 2026.

supported_claims[1]:
2.1: Domains: engineering-rule retrieval/application, technical-document understanding, vehicle-drawing understanding. 2.2: Area: AI evaluation using engineering tasks. 2.3: Intended assessed population: AI systems. 2.4: Intended user professions are not explicitly specified.

supported_claims[2]:
2.5: Six task groups: individual-rule retrieval, related-rule retrieval, technical-term explanation, component presence, dimensional compliance and functional performance. Their scores are not established as distinct underlying skills.

supported_claims[3]:
2.6: Response mode: generated text, yes/no and sometimes explanations. 2.8: Instructions and settings are described in the paper; some systems receive a whole rulebook and others retrieved passages.

supported_claims[4]:
2.9: Open production and binary selection responses. 2.10: Written rules, vehicle images and drawings. 2.11: 1,451 question-answer pairs; individual-rule retrieval has 1,192 and functional performance has 16. Counts for the other four groups are not supplied.

supported_claims[5]:
2.15: Passage, dimension-label, scale-bar and image-highlighting conditions were examined; these are not established equivalent forms. 2.16: The original question collection is fixed; retrieval changes supplied information. 2.17: Other informant: the AI supplies assessed responses; engineers and researchers contributed benchmark materials.

supported_claims[6]:
3.1: Digital scoring using public software. 3.2: Text similarity and correct yes/no decisions are used, with some explanations separately scored. The software gives each of six groups equal overall weight. 3.3: Other scales: task-specific similarity/accuracy and an equally weighted composite.

supported_claims[7]:
5.1: Public questions, instructions, scoring code, some AI responses and small marking-test files are described. 5.2: A paper and public digital releases are available; exact publication formats are not fully specified.

supported_claims[8]:

AI systems retrieve and apply rules, explain terms and interpret images or drawings. Scoring combines several methods and equally weights groups. Results describe systems together with their information supply; broader engineering-document competence remains uncertain.

supported_claims[9]:
6.1.1 = 2: The intended connection between task performance and engineering-document understanding is explained, with limited theoretical elaboration. 6.1.2 = 2: Model results and condition changes provide empirical observations, without comprehensive construct research.

supported_claims[10]:

supported_claims[11]:

supported_claims[12]:

supported_claims[13]:

supported_claims[14]:

supported_claims[16]:

supported_claims[17]:

documented_problems[0]:
2.11, 6.1.3.1: Task groups are highly uneven: 1,192 individual-rule questions versus 16 performance questions. Equal group weighting gives these groups equal composite influence without supplied measurement justification.

documented_problems[1]:
3.2, 7.1.7: Documented examples show missing commas and valid related rules absent from supplied answers affecting credit. This establishes some construct-irrelevant scoring sensitivity, not its overall frequency.

documented_problems[2]:

documented_problems[3]:
9.7, 10.3.1.6: Five passage sets for one AI provide condition-variation evidence, not identical-test repeatability. One additional correct response changes the 16-question group's accuracy by 6.25 percentage points, as stated in the passage.

documented_problems[4]:
10.4, 11: All described scale-bar drawings comply. Always answering yes would obtain their decision credit; this is an inferred vulnerability, not evidence that any tested AI exploited it.

documented_problems[5]:

documented_problems[6]:
5.1, 6.2.2: Revisions are identifiable in code history, but a clear account of their score effects was not found in the reviewed materials.

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 evaluates AI performance on unfamiliar coloured-grid transformations inferred from examples. This review covers the public test problems, inspected official scoring software and ARC Prize verified-testing rules described in the supplied passage. Evidence supports a defined grid-task comparison; broader reasoning interpretations remain unresolved. The original EFPA 2025 model is retained, with explicit adaptations for AI assessment. Section ratings are judgements, not averages; no aggregate quality score is calculated.

reinterpretations[12]:
Final evaluation and Conclusions: Precision and validity of broader reasoning interpretations are critical qualities. Under EFPA’s rule, their 0 ratings restrict those interpretations to research or exceptional expert use and leave them below the model’s minimum evidential standard. Descriptive reporting of observed task scores remains supportable. Supplier qualification requirements and future research plans are unknown; ongoing material corrections are documented. No numbered items are omitted; grouped entries share the stated rationale.

closing_note:
Unclear questions/instructions: distinguish average fractional problem score from fully solved problem count, and identify the exact version, run settings and grid representation. The supplied example explains fractional scoring, but does not establish that all original instructions are clear.

instrument_review: DesignQA is reviewed as a benchmark of AI performance on questions about a Formula SAE rulebook and vehicle materials, under particular information-supply and scoring conditions. Its tasks have practical engineering relevance, while scoring artefacts, uneven task coverage and incomplete precision evidence limit broader interpretations. This review applies EFPA 2025 Parts A–C, retaining its item IDs and rating meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section ratings are judgements, not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated. Only the supplied passages were used; the original PDF and benchmark sources were not independently inspected.
closing_note: Unclear questions/instructions: valid related rules missing from reference answers, punctuation-sensitive credit and different supplied passages complicate what counts as a correct, comparable response. The passages do not identify every ambiguous question; exact historical prompts and inputs are also incompletely linked to results.

instrument_review:
DesignQA is reviewed as a benchmark of AI performance on questions about a Formula SAE rulebook and vehicle materials, under particular information-supply and scoring conditions. Its tasks have practical engineering relevance, while scoring artefacts, uneven task coverage and incomplete precision evidence limit broader interpretations. This review applies EFPA 2025 Parts A–C, retaining its item IDs and rating meanings: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Section ratings are judgements, not averages. No aggregate quality score is calculated. Only the supplied passages were used; the original PDF and benchmark sources were not independently inspected.

documented_problems[0]:
2.11, 6.1.3.1 = 1; 6.1.3.3 = 1: One rulebook and limited task types constrain coverage of broad engineering-document understanding. documented_problems[1]:
3.2, 6.3.2 = 1: Wording and formatting can alter credit, including missing commas and valid related rules absent from reference answers. These documented cases compromise the alignment between credit and substantive correctness.

documented_problems[2]:
3.2, 10.5: Equal group weighting combines different marking methods and gives small groups substantial influence. This is a transparent scoring choice, but its interpretation as a distinct overall engineering skill is unvalidated.

documented_problems[3]:

documented_problems[5]:

documented_problems[6]:
9.7: Five passage sets for one AI provide limited variation evidence, but changing passages does not isolate repeatability under identical conditions. A single answer in the 16-question group changes accuracy by 6.25 percentage points.

documented_problems[7]:

documented_problems[8]:

documented_problems[9]:
5, 6.3.8: Code revisions are identifiable, but no clear record explaining score effects was found in the reviewed material. A licence file and complete reuse rules were also not found; this does not establish that reuse is prohibited.

instrument_review:
EFPA 2025 review of ARC-AGI-2 public test problems, official scoring software and ARC Prize verified-testing rules, limited to the supplied passages. The benchmark presents example input/output grids and asks AI systems to generate outputs for unfamiliar inputs. Scores describe exact-output success under specified conditions. Human difficulty matching supports puzzle selection but does not establish AI measurement equivalence, precision or broader intelligence. All numbered descriptive fields and evaluative items are addressed below, with grouping only where explicit IDs share a rationale. Section-level overall ratings are judgements, not averages; no aggregate quality score is calculated.

documented_problems[3]:

Broader reasoning and intelligence interpretations remain unresolved, and small ranking differences lack demonstrated repeatability.

documented_problems[2]:

documented_problems[3]:

documented_problems[4]:

documented_problems[5]:

reinterpretations[0]:
Rating key retained: n/a = inapplicable; 0 = insufficient information; 1 = inadequate; 2 = adequate; 3 = good; 4 = excellent. Missing evidence is not evidence of poor performance. Section ratings use judgement, not arithmetic averaging.

reinterpretations[1]:
Part A and sections 6–12 retain their original purposes. Test taker means the AI system with its configured interface and evaluation conditions; users are its evaluators. This adaptation does not equate an AI score with a human psychological trait.

reinterpretations[2]:
2.7, 7.1.6, 11: Human sensory, motor and disability questions are explicitly separated from AI input compatibility. Fair use is considered as defensible comparison across systems, interfaces and conditions; human demographic fairness is not inferred.

reinterpretations[3]:
8: The original model permits argued exceptions to norm requirements. That exception is used only for descriptive raw-performance comparison; intelligence norms, competence thresholds and classifications remain unsupported.

reinterpretations[4]:
9: Repeated testing concerns a fixed AI configuration under fixed conditions. Human difficulty matching, training changes and software correctness answer different questions from score precision.

reinterpretations[5]:
4, 12: Numeric outputs and public archives are not silently treated as psychological interpretation reports. Their existence does not resolve whether the original report criteria apply.

reinterpretations[6]:
Critical attributes: 9.8 and 10.5 are critical for defensible score interpretation; broader reasoning interpretations have insufficient external validation. A critical 0 triggers the original exceptional-expert/research-use guidance without proving the benchmark itself inadequate.

reinterpretations[7]:
Coverage: Every supplied numbered descriptive field and rated item is addressed, including conditional subareas. Parent headings organize their children without invented extra ratings. The summary table's reference to 7.2.8 conflicts with the supplied substantive section, which ends at 7.2.7; 7.2.7 is used and no nonexistent item is invented.

reinterpretations[8]:
Instrument attribution: Adapted application of EFPA's original 2025 model, supplied as CC BY-SA 4.0. The supplied extraction was used; the authoritative PDF was not inspected. This review implies no EFPA endorsement.

closing_note:
Unclear questions/instructions: 'solved' must distinguish exact input success, fractional problem credit and fully solved problems. Exact AI input encoding and complete administration instructions are unavailable, so their clarity remains unresolved.

instrument_review: DesignQA samples AI answers to Formula SAE rules and vehicle-material questions across six groups. Its practical source materials support relevance to those tasks, but scoring sensitivity, unequal information supply and incomplete precision evidence limit interpretation of rankings and broader engineering competence. This recorded AI review simulation applies the supplied original EFPA 2025 model, retaining its numbered fields and technical areas. No aggregate quality score is calculated.
closing_note: Unclear questions/instructions: Acceptable wording, formatting and inclusion of related rules need clearer scoring guidance. Full item text is unavailable, so individual-question ambiguity cannot be comprehensively assessed; training and repeated-submission rules are also insufficiently clear.

instrument_review:
DesignQA samples AI answers to Formula SAE rules and vehicle-material questions across six groups. Its practical source materials support relevance to those tasks, but scoring sensitivity, unequal information supply and incomplete precision evidence limit interpretation of rankings and broader engineering competence. This recorded AI review simulation applies the supplied original EFPA 2025 model, retaining its numbered fields and technical areas. No aggregate quality score is calculated.

documented_problems[7]:

instrument_review:
ARC-AGI-2 is reviewed using the supplied EFPA 2025 model, with AI systems replacing human test takers only where explicitly stated below. The evidence supports a bounded interpretation of scores as exact grid-output performance under specified evaluation conditions. It does not establish repeatability, equivalent measurement across AI configurations, or general intelligence. Every numbered descriptive field and rated item is addressed below; no items are intentionally omitted. Section ratings are judgements, not averages, and no aggregate quality score is calculated.

supported_claims[0]:
1: Instrument name and short name: ARC-AGI-2. Developers: ARC Prize Foundation staff and partners; the example figure credits François Chollet and colleagues. Source inspection: 7 October 2026, which is not a publication or review date.

supported_claims[1]:
2.1: Content keywords: rule inference, grid problems, reasoning. 2.2: Area: AI benchmarking and reasoning research. 2.3: Intended population: AI systems; eligibility boundaries are not specified. 2.4: Intended users: researchers comparing AI systems, inferred from the stated use.

supported_claims[2]:
2.5: One reported problem-averaged performance score; no separate scores established as distinct skills. 2.6: Responses are output grids represented through the evaluation software. 2.8: Verified evaluations specify AI settings, a spending limit and one run; other routes may differ.

supported_claims[3]:
2.9: Production-based grid responses scored for exact success. 2.10: Coloured two-dimensional grids. 2.11: 1,000 development problems and three 120-problem evaluation sets; problems may have multiple new inputs. 2.12.1: Individual-system assessment is the applicable interpretation. 2.12.2: Verified testing is controlled automated administration; other routes vary.

supported_claims[4]:
2.15: Public, semi-private and private evaluation sets differ in access and were matched for human difficulty; ARC-AGI-1 and ARC-AGI-2 are separate versions. 2.16: Released problem sets are fixed; no adaptive administration is described. 2.17: The evaluated AI produces the responses; these are performance responses, not psychological self-reports.

supported_claims[5]:
3.1: Digital scoring of submitted outputs. 3.2: Up to two attempts per new input; an exact match earns credit, input credits are averaged within each problem, and problem scores are then averaged. 3.3: Raw proportion scores. 3.4: Standard-score transformation is not applicable. 3.5: No differentiated norms are described.

supported_claims[6]:
5.1: Available supporting materials include a technical report, public problems, running software, marking tests, evaluation rules and a change record. 5.2: Public digital materials are described. documented_problems[2]:

Their remaining extent is not established. 7.1.8=2: Examples, public materials and corrections support basic material adequacy, while robustness and full item-quality evidence remain unavailable.

documented_problems[3]:
8.3.2.1: Corrected problems and code changes can affect score comparability. The change record does not recalculate every affected AI score; no normative distortion is established.

documented_problems[4]:
9.4: Human difficulty matching does not demonstrate alternate-form equivalence for AI systems.

documented_problems[5]:
10.4: Public evaluation problems permit prior exposure. Hidden-test agreements and monitoring mitigate exposure but acknowledge possible escape; they do not establish absence of contamination.

documented_problems[6]:
Final evaluation: Strengths include transparent scoring logic, inspectable public materials, content review and tracked corrections. One-run verified testing, unquantified score variation and unresolved exposure limit comparative conclusions. Under EFPA's critical-attribute guidance, the critical 9.8=0 confines supported use to research or exceptional expert-led interpretation; it does not prove poor repeatability.

instrument_review:
Condition-native review using the complete original EFPA Test Review Model 2025, version 5.0. Part A: 1: Reviewer perspective is benchmark review; reviewer identity and review date are unspecified. Sources were inspected on 6 October 2026; this is not a previous review date. Instrument: original DesignQA benchmark described in the 2024 paper and its public scoring software. Authors are described as researchers and engineers; individual names, publisher/distributor, exact original publication date, current revision date, adaptation authors and adaptation dates are unspecified. No local adaptation is identified. 2: Classification is described below. 2.1: Keywords: engineering-rule retrieval, drawing interpretation, rule application. 2.2: AI evaluation using engineering materials. 2.3: AI systems; narrower eligibility is unspecified. 2.4: Researchers and evaluators are implied; supplier-defined user qualifications are unspecified. 2.5: Six question-group scores and an equal-weight overall score; distinct underlying skill measurement is unestablished. 2.6: Machine-generated text or yes/no responses, sometimes with explanations. 2.7: Human attention, handedness, hearing and motor capabilities are inapplicable. Human language command, fluency, digital experience, reading, vision and writing become model/interface prerequisites; their limitations are not fully specified. Other demands include accessing supplied rules and interpreting technical drawings. 2.8: Instructions and settings are described, with whole-rulebook versus retrieved-passage conditions differing across systems. 2.9: Open text and binary decisions, sometimes with explanations. 2.10: Written rules, vehicle images and drawings. 2.11: 1,451 question-answer pairs in six groups; 1,192 individual-rule questions and 16 performance questions. Other group counts are not supplied. 2.12.1: Individual AI-system evaluation; human group administration is inapplicable. 2.12.2: Public materials; supervision, identity controls and protected evaluation arrangements are not established. 2.13: Digital execution is implied; specific hardware/connectivity requirements are unavailable. 2.14: Preparation, administrator involvement, analysis and feedback times are unspecified; scoring is automated, so manual scoring time is zero, while computation time is unspecified. 2.15: Different information-supply and image variants are studied, without demonstrated parallel-form equivalence; later revisions may affect results. 2.16: Public questions are a fixed set; adaptive item selection is not described. 2.17: The AI provides task responses, not human self-report. 3: Measurement and scoring are described below. 3.1: Automated scoring using answer comparison and binary correctness. 3.2: Group-specific methods include text similarity and yes/no accuracy; the software equally weights six groups. No common psychometric calibration or guessing correction is established. 3.3: Raw accuracy/similarity and their composite; no established standard scores or critical decision thresholds. 3.4: Standard-score transformation is inapplicable. 3.5: No differentiated norms are documented. 4: Automated numerical outputs are provisionally treated as digital reports. 4.1: Scoring software produces group and overall scores; report types and their number are unspecified. 4.2: Group and overall evaluation outputs. 4.3: Presentation format is unspecified. 4.4: Question-group and composite structure. 4.5: Audience/context adaptation is unspecified. 4.6: Metric computation and equal weighting are described; interpretive narrative development is unspecified. 4.7: Modifiability is unspecified. 4.8: Aggregation is described, but score-to-competence linkage is unestablished. 4.9: Task performance descriptions; diagnostic or predictive reporting is unspecified. 4.10: Researchers and evaluators are implied recipients; formal recipient categories are unspecified. 5: Supply arrangements are described below. 5.1: Paper, public questions, instructions, scoring code, small marking-test files and some AI responses are described. 5.2: Public digital materials. 5.3: Supplier-required qualifications are unspecified. General description: DesignQA evaluates AI responses to Formula SAE rules, vehicle images and drawings through six task groups: individual-rule retrieval, related-rule retrieval, technical terminology, component presence, dimensional compliance and functional performance. Its 1,451 questions are highly unevenly distributed across groups. Different marking methods are combined into an equal-weight overall score. Reported model conditions differ in information supply, and the public materials do not fully reconstruct every historical result. The benchmark supports examination of performance on these tasks under stated conditions; transfer to other technical documents remains uncertain. Part B: Item ratings and reasons appear below. Final evaluation: Practical materials support task relevance, while documented scoring and design issues weaken interpretation of the composite as engineering understanding. Precision and transfer evidence are insufficient. Part C: Sources are limited to the supplied benchmark passage and supplied EFPA extraction; underlying documents were not independently examined.
